Ladies and Gentlemen,
 The _past week has brought us some military surprises, accompanied by political and diplomatic developements, Since we are approching mid-winter, nothing of a decisive character is likely to happen, But the events of the week are all the same of considerable importance, in so far as they are indicative of the future.
 The military situation in south-eastern Russia has produced the chief surprise. The Swiss Observer. Mon.Nov.9th.1942. 
Military history has been eventful during the past week. At 
the end of October the war seemed to be settling down into 
a period of routine fighting with only the usual ups and downs. 
But the first week of November has produced new deielopments 
whose repercussions may reach far in the near future. 
To begin with, the Russian campaign seems to have stagnated - 
and that means a considerable advantage for the Soviet armies 
and a disappointment for the Axis forces. Street-fighting in 
Stalingrad continues, and the Wehrmacht isistill advancing into 
the Caucasian mountains, but neither control of the Volga nor 
access to Trans-Caucasia appears to be within reach. At the most, 
défensive advantages are being secured - and those at a price 
which may prove out of proportion to the results achieved. [...]

The fourth War-Christmas has been very different 
from the Christmas-Feasts of the three first years of the war. Whereas 
in 1939 it was still celebrated in the somewhat careless athmosphere 
of the War-that-is-no-War, it had assumed a grim aspect in 1940 because 
it granted but a few days respite during the Battle of Britain; and 
whereas in 1941, Christmas again brought a lull in the storm declenched 
by Japan in the Far East, it almost remained unnoticed on the battlefields

and Africa, that no pause was possible in order to remember the devine

The Swiss Observer. Mon.Dec.21st.1942. 
An eventful week lies behind us. Military events are taking 
their inexorable course, and the political situation resembles 
a game of chess, with prudent moves and reckless counter-strokes 
prompted by the temperament or strategic position of the 
antagonists. 
The African campaign has become a race to Tripolis between 
General Montgomery and Marshal Rommel. Only a week has passed 
since the Allies took the initiative on the Tripolitan frontier, 
and they are already within sight of Syrte, roughly halfway 
between Benghazi and Italy's colonial capital. The Axis

abstract:
Topic of the day. Talk of Monday, October 2nd 1939. 
Ladies and gentlemen, 
I am sure that I need not tell you hos sorry Switzerland is 
about the new"partage"of Poland. We sympathise deeply with this 
nation, which has, for centuries fought for indépendance and freedom. 
Again and again this country had to submit to foreign dominatio 
and we admire thèse men who have fought with such courage for a 
cause, which, from the very beginning, was doamed to be lost. They 
fought to save the honour of their country, a thing of which many 
to-day are quite unmindful.

Ladies and Gentlemen, 
You are not unaware of the role played in contemporaneous European 
affairs by the propaganda of the major states. In fact, the importance of 
this role could scarcely be exaggerated. One of the reasons for this is 
that these campaigns are not assigned objectives which are only political 
in nature. They are not simply an effort to justify, in the minds of the 
state's own citizens, and, at the same time, in the minds of citizens of 
other states, the territorial or economical aspirations and ambitions 
of the country which launches them.

Ladies and Gentlemen, 
Just now when the League of Nations is meeting in regular assembly on 
Swiss territory, it is perhaps not unnecessary to restate before the world

Tagosüberblick von Freitag,den 4.September 1942. Raeber. 
Auf dem Gebiete der internationalen Politik sind heut« die beiden 
Hauptthemata der Diskussion die gestrige Rede von Praesident Roosevelt 
sowie die ebenfalls gestern spaet bekanntgewordene Umbildung der spanischen 
Regierung. 
Aus den Darlegungen Roosevelts wird besonders die Erklärung des 
Praesidenten festgehalten,dass der Kampf lang und hart sein werde,dass aber 
die Alliierten hierfür sowohl die technischen Mittel als auch den erforderlichen 
Mut besaessen.Es gehe um die Freiheit der Welt,es gehe darum, diesmal 
bei Kriegsende einen wirklichen Frieden zu sichern und zu verhindern,dass

The Swiss constitution, which is the fundamental law of our land, traces its 
origin back to the year 1848. At that time the existing union of sovereign cantons 
was transformed into a confederated State. Barely over a quarter of a

segment_title: Swiss liberty under a full powers regime
abstract:
Swiss liberty under a full powers régime A . A ¿ JL 
The Swiss Confederation is a democracy of a special nature. Its constitution 
grants citizens - as do the constitutions of other democratic states - a number 
of clearly defined liberties, such as freedom of faith and conscience, freedom 
of the press, and the freedom to organize political parties. In the majority of 
the cantons that make up the Confederation, Swiss citizens elect their parliaments 
and their governments. And in addition to this power of election, the 
Swiss people have the right to decide changes in constitution and law. This last 
privilege is the most vital characteristic of Swiss democracy. As a matter of 
fact, the Swiss people, of all peoples on earth, enjoy, from a constitutional 
viewpoint, the most extensive liberties and rights. 
These facts are well known. [...]

SWITZERLAND MODIFIES BER ERIVATE LIFE 
Visitors from other parts of the continent usually consider Switzerland to 
be a paradise, since relatively little apparent change is seen in pre-war privileges 
as far as our private lives are concerned. This opinion is, however, 
superficial. For this to he readily understood we have only to mention that 
nearly all food products - the exceptions are fresh vegetables and popatoes -

have blackout from 8 p.m.'; and last, but not least, the cost of living has gone 
up 5o % since 1939Ï All this has profoundly modified the private life of every

Switzerland's Pood Situation. Wed.June 3rd. 1943. DU/ld 
Federal Councillor Stampfli, the head of our economic department, 
recently referred in a public speech to the country's food 
situation. He pointed out that all the ships of the Swiss mercantile 
marine are at the present lying uselessly at anchor in ports 
of the Iberian Peninsula . We have to go without the cargoes 
they should be bringing us - not only raw materials, but grain 
for bread, edible oils and fats, coffee and sugar. M.Stampfli 
shewed what serious consequences a prolongation of this state of 
affairs must have upon our food supplies.

06.06.1943 
The problem of a protecting power
 
The Problems of a Protecting Power 
One very important duty neutral Switzerland has taken upon herself 
for the duration of the war is that devolving upon a protecting power. 
In fact, this rôle has taken on such vast proportions that it can truly 
be said that Switzerland has gathered up the last threads which remain of 
international relations. But the task which has fallen upon our country 
is being done without ostentation: rather with that quiet modesty which 
becomes a sincere tribute to the fellowship of nations today so bitterly 
torn asunder. To be sure, there is nothing of a sensational character in 
the duties ofa protecting power. There is, on the contrary, much detail

Switzerland and the right of asylum 
A somewhat uneasy feeling was created recently in Switzerland when 
the American and British foreign departments requested our government 
to refuse certain persons the right of asylum in Switzerland, should 
this privilege be asked for. They said, in fact, that to grant such

infringment upon our sovereign rights. Every independent State, whether

The Swiss Colonies abroad after 4 years of war. 
Every year it is the custom of delegates from the various Swiss 
colonies abroad to meet in some pleasant spot of Switzerland 
to resume contact with representative authorities of the home 
country and exchange ideas and impressions. Before the war,

20,000 ITALIAN REFUGEES IN SWITZERLAND 
After the capitulation of Italy, about 2o,ooo Italian military and civil 
refugees and some l,ooo escaped Allied prisoners poured into Switzerland. This 
naturally created problems which had to be dealt with by the competent ministry of 
Justice and Police. 
Federal Councilor de Steiger has given a detailed report in parliament about 
this refugee influx. Switzerland now has nearly 60,000 emigrants and refugees within 
her borders, which represents 1 - % of her entire population. This would mean, 
for England, half a million people, and for the United States 1 and a half million. 
The number is indeed considerable for a little country like Switzerland, especially 
now that she is so to speak cut off from all overseas communications and must give 
much attention to questions of food, shelter, clothing and employment. [...]

abstract:

  During the last session of the Federal Assembly, a debate of particular importance 
took place before the National Council. We believe this debate to be worthy of a word 
of explanation and 'comment with our overseas friends in mind. 
Outwardly, the discussions concerned a motion to appoint a special Constitutional 
Commission in case &M a total revision of the Confederation's constitution should be 
deemed necessary. The National Council rejected this proposal by a strong majority: 
129 votes against 9. Judging from the general course of the debate, it would seem that 
the representatives of the people do not feel that a total revision of the constitution 
is recommendable; in fact, they apparently found it absolutely unnecessary end undesirable

Does it sound thoughtless and light-hearted to think of war - which carries 
in its wake so much horror and distress - as a means of education ? And yet 
we know to what extent suffering of all kinds fulfills an educational mission

Wie aus Berliner militärischen Kreisen zum Krieg in Russland verlautet, 
treten an der Ostfront Tier grosse Schwerpunkte in Erscheinung. Der 
erste Schv/erpunkt liege südwestlieh ron Narra, wo schwere Kämpfe 
mit rassischen Divisionen im Gange seien. Die deutschen Führung habe 
neue Reserven herangeführt und es entwickle sieh eine grosse Schlacht, 
hei der vor allem der Artillerie besondere Bedeutung zukomme* Nordwestlich 
Nevel liege der zweite Schwerpunkt und im Räume von Bogatschew 
der dritte. Der Gegner versuche dort mit allen Mitteln einen Durchbruch 
nach Bobruisk zu erzwingen» Der letzte Schwerpunkt liege im Südabschnit  
bei Kriwoy Bog«

Swiss Commercial Policy 
in Wartime 
B - b
There is barely another country where the foreign commercial policy brings 
up as many complicated problems as in Switzerland. Our land has no direct 
access to the sea and is completely surrounded by the Axis. In order to live, 
we must import from overseas, and for this, navycerts have to be obtained from 
London. At the same time, when the goods finally do arrive in Marseilles, we must 
have the authorization of the Axis to transport them inland across occupied 
Prance. 
Of course, Switzerland must also be able to export, otherwise she can get 
nothing from abroad. And this export trade, in turn, is of the most vital 
interest to warfaring countries. Switzerland has international transit lines,

abstract:
Der Aufschwung des Schweizer Buchs.
Je weiter die Zerstörungen in Europe fortschreiten, desto mehr entwickelt sich der Aufschwung des Schweizer Buchs. Die beiden grossen Bücherlieferanten des Schweiz, Deutschland und Frankreich, fallen praktisch fast aus. In Leipzig sollen die grossen Verlage und Bücherstocks vernichtet sein. Mit grosser Tatkraft sind die Verleger der Schweiz auf allen Gebieten, den wissenschaftlichen, Schulbüchern, Klassikerausgaben, der schönen Literatur und sogar der schwierigen Musikpartituren in die Lacke gesprungen. Im Jahre 1943 haben die Verlage der Schweiz 3358 Werke herausgebracht, 500 mehr als 1942 und 800 mehr als 1941. […]

segment_title: Swiss books come into their own
abstract:
SWISS BOOKS COME INTO THEIR OWN
The more destruction abounds in Europe , the more the demand for Swiss books.
The two great book-furnishing countries of Switzerland, Germany and France, can practical ly no longer be reckoned with. In Leipzig the large publishing houses and
book reserve stocks have been dstroyed , we are told. Very energetically the publishers in Switzerland have tried to fill the gap   with Swiss production s along all lines: scientific works, school books, classical literature, poetry and even difficult
music partitions . In 1943, the 3wiss publishing houses brought out 3,358 works, 500 more than in 1942 and 800 more than in 1941.

We, Swiss, have noted with lively interest the passage in President

abstract:
ARE THE SWISS IMPATIENT? 
May 23, 1945 B b. 
/ 
As can readily be understood, discussion in Switzerland centers at the present 
time on the doing- away with the measures brought about by the war. The Swiss people 
have consented to many secrifices and to very severe restrictions in behalf of their 
country's defense, but now they are again filled with a strong craving after liberty. 
First of all, the soldiers expect that henceforth only the most essential border and
